quotes.text: While Levine and Carmichael were in New York, they began to take notice of the urban music surrounding them and later let the style influence the songs they wrote.
When the band returned in 2001, they brought those influences with them.

From this point forward, most Maroon 5 songs would be Maroon 5 songs in the same way that "Call Me" was a Blondie song despite just being Debbie Harry and Giorgio Moroder. Adam Levine was the only Maroon who mattered.

This time around, the band enlisted a different historically important mega-producer, but this one was a little more attuned to the times. The producer was Max Martin, and being attuned to the times meant making a bunch of forgettable, frictionless pop songs that basically served as Adam Levine solo records in all but name.
Once he decided that he was fine with Maroon 5 just becoming his dance-pop project, that decision probably got a whole lot easier.
But for the most part, the record is what happens when Adam Levine goes into the lab with the biggest pop names that he can round up.

Early in their career, Maroon 5 hit upon a sort of agreeable, easy-to-ignore blue-eyed-soul thing, and they tweaked that formula over the years, somehow riding the zeitgeist and usually staying somewhere near the top of the pop charts.
Maroon 5's music just slips past me, into the ether. These songs are ghosts; they leave no footprints.
The members of Maroon 5 are simply professionals with sharp instincts who rode all their built-in advantages as hard as they could.
"Makes Me Wonder," Maroon 5's first chart-topper, doesn't do much else, but it puts their smooth and precise mediocrity on full display.

Maroon 5 were a rock band once. At the tail end of the '90s alt-rock boom, Maroon 5 had a label deal and an album. They were spectacularly unsuccessful, and maybe that experience led them to become the slipstream hitmakers that they are now.
The Fourth World sounded like a group of talented, ambitious kids attempting to make a Weezer record and failing.

Back in LA, Levine and Carmichael got back together with Kara's Flowers, and the band tried recording more songs. There, they got into rap and R&B, and they only lasted one semester before dropping out.
The idea behind the new member was that it would allow Adam Levine, still a shy reluctant-frontman type, to stop playing rhythm guitar and to get out front and move around.

Maroon 5 started off their career as a Pop/Rock/Funk band back in the very early 2000s and brought us the masterpiece debut album 'Songs About Jane'. 15 year later the band is still going strong with the newest album called 'Red Pill Blues'. The resemblance between these two albums is relatively zero. The Rock/Funk part of the band is non-existent and all you have is glorified POP!
This album seems to be one electronica, synthesizer made record.
I'm of the opinion that they've sorta became a vehicle for Adam Levine to get his R n' B thing out.
It's okay to reinvent yourself; it's just in the case of Maroon 5, they just became so unoriginal and generic.
They reinvented themselves into a lesser band. Not a good reinvention.
